Of Foxing or Tainting Malt-Liquors.

Foxing .is a misfortune, or rather a disease, in maltdrinks, occasioned by divers means, as the nastiness of the utensils, putting the worts too thick together in the backs or coolers, brewing toooften and soon one after another, and sometimes by bad masts and waters, and the liquors taken in wrong heats, being of such pernicious consequence to the great brewer in particular, that he sometimes cannot recover and bring his matters into a right order again in lefs than a week or two, and is so hateful to him in its very name, that it is a general law among them to make all servants that name the word Fox or Foxing in the brew-house to pay six-pence, which obliges them to call it Reynard ; for, when once the drink is tainted, it may be smelt at lbrne diilance somewhat like a Fox : It chiefly happens in hot weather, and caufes the beer and ale so tainted to acquire a fulsome sickish taste, that will, if it is received in a great degree, become ropy like treacle, and in some sliort time turn four.

And here we /hall mention the great value of the hop in preventing and curing the fox in malt-liquors. When the wort is run into the tub out of the mashing-vat, it is a very good way to throw some hops diredUy into it be fore it is put into the copper, and they will secure it against sourness and ropiness, that are the two effects of foxed worts or drinks, and are of such power in this respect, that raw worts may be kept some time, even in hot weather, before they are boiled, and which is necessary where there is a large quantity of malt used to a little copper; but it is certain that the stronger worts will keep longer with hops than the smaller forts: So Jikewise, if a person has fewer tubs than are wanted, and he is apprehenilve his worts will be foxed by too thick lying in the coolers or working tubs, then it will be a safe way to put some fresh hops into such tubs, and work them with the yeast, of, in cafe the drink is already foxed in the vat or tun, new hops should be put in and worked with it, and they will greatly fetch it again into a right order ; but then such drink Ihould be carefully taken clear off from its gross nasty lee, which being mostly tainted, would otherwise lie in the barrel, corrupt, and make it worse.

Some fift quick-lime into foxed drinks while they are working in the tun or vat, that its fire and fait may break the cohesions of the beer or ale, and burn away the stench that the corruption would always cause ; but then such drink should by a peg at the bottom of the vat be drawn off as fine as possible, and the dregs left behind.

Though a fin all quantity of yeast be necessary to ferment and fine the wort ; yet it is in itself of a poisonous nature, and if beat into the wort too often or in too large a quantity, by its stupifying and narcotic quality, it makes the liquor so heady, that five bushels of malt maybe equal in strength to fix. But liquor made in this manner is extremely unwholfome.

Of 'working and fermenting London Stout Beer and Ale ,

The yeast is at once put into the tun to work the stout-beer and ale with ; by this means, and the /shortness of time we have to ferment our strong drinks, we cannot make reserves of cold worts to mix with and check the too forward working of those liquors. The strong beer brewed for keeping is suffered to be blood-warm in the winter, when the yeast is put into it, that it may gradually work two nights and a day at least, for this will not admit of such a, IvJty operation as the common brown ale, because, if it is worked too warm and hasty, such b.ear will not keep near so long as that fermented cooler. The brown ale has, indeed, its yeast put into it in the evening very warm, because it is often carried away the very next morning. The pale or amber ales are often kept near it, not quite a week under fermentation, for the better incorporating the yeast with the wort.

Of forwarding and retard big the Fermentation of Maltliquors.

In cafe beer or ale is backward in working, it is customary to cast some flour out of the dusting-box, or with the hand, over the top of the drink, which will become a sort of crust or cover to help to keep the cold out : Others put in one or two ounces of powdered ginger, which heats the wort and brings it forward : Others take a gallon stone-bottle and fill it with boiling water, which, being well corked, is put into the working tub, where it communicates a gradual heat for some time, and forwards the fermentation : Others reserve some raw wort, which they heat and mix with the reft ; but then care must be taken, that the pot in which it is heated has no manner of grease about it, left it Ihould injpede, instead of promoting the working ; but, for retarding and keeping back any drink that is too much heated in working, the cold raw wort is the most proper of any thing to check it ; though some are known to put one or more pewter difties into it for that purpose ; or, it may be broke intofeveral other tubs, where, by its /hallow lying, its fury will be abated. Others again, to make drink work that is backward, will take the whites ot two eggs, and beat them up with half a quartern of good brandy, and put it either into the working-vat, or into the ca/k, which will quickly bring it forward, if a warm cloth is put over the bung. Others tie up bran in a coarse thin cloth, and put it into the vat, where, by its spongy nature, it absorbs a quantity of the drink, and breeds a heat to forward its working.

Of artificial Lees for Stout or Stale Beer to _ feed on.

This article is of very great importance in the curing of our malt-liquors. The general misfortune of the porter or keeping-beers drinking hard and hart ti, is partly owing to the nasty soul feces that lie at the bottom of the calk, compounded of the sediments of malt, hops, and yeast. Wheat is, by many, put into such beer to feed and preserve it, as being reckoned a substantial alcali; however, it has been proved, that such wheat in about three years time has eat into the very wood of the caflc. Others hang a bag of wheat in the vessel, that it may not touch the bottom ; but, in both cafes, the wheat is discovered to absorb and collet the acid qualities of the beer, yeast, and hop. Hence' it is, that such whole wheat is loaded w ith the qualities of the unwholesome settlements or grounds of the beer, and becomes of such a corroding nature, as to do mischief; and, for that reason, some hang a bag of the flour of malted oats, wheat, pease, or beans, in the vessels of beer, as being of a lighter and mellower body than the whole wheat or its flour, and more natural to the liquor : But whether it be raw wheat or malted, it is supposed, after this receptacle has emitted its alcalous properties to the beer, and taken in all it can of the acid qualities thereof, that such beer will in time prey upon that again, and so communicate its pernicious qualities to the liquor.

Composition for feeding Porter or Keeping-Beers.

Take a quart of French brandy, or as much of English, that is free from any burnt tang, or other ill taste, and is full proof; to this put as much wheat or bean flour as will knead it into dough, put it in long pieces "into the bung-hole, as soon as the beer has done working, or afterwards, and let it gently fall piece by piece to the bottom of the butt ; this will maintain the diink in a mellow freshness, keep staleness off for some time, and cause it to be the stronger as it grows aged.

Another.

Take one pound of treacle, or honey, one pound of the powder of dried oyster-shells, .or fat chalk, mix them well, and put it into a butt, as soon as it has done working, or some time after, and bung it well ; this will both fine and preserve the beer in a soft, smooth condition for a great while.

In each barrel-copper of wort, put in two quarts of whole wheat as soon as possible, that it may soak before it boils ; then strain it through a sieve, and put the wort in cooling-tubs : Thus there will be extracted a gluey consistence, which, being incorporated with the wort by boiling, gives it a more thick and ponderous body, and, when in the caflt, soon makes a sediment or lee, as. the wort is more or lefs loaded with the weighty particles of this sizy body; but if the wheat were first parched, or baked in an oven, it would do better, as being rather too raw as it comes from the ear.

Of the Cellar or Repository for keeping Beers and Ases.

Tr is' certain, that the weather has not only a power or influence in brewing, but also after die diink is in the barrel, hogshead, or butt, in cellars, or other places, which is often the cause of forwarding or retarding the ficenefs of malt-liquors ; for if we brew iB cold weather, and the drink is to stand in a cellar of clay, or where springs rife, or waters lie or pass through such a place, rise se will check the due course of the drink, chill, flat, deaden, and hinder it from becoming fine. Sa likewise, if beer or ale. is brewed in hot weather, and put into chalky, gravelly, or sandy cellars, and especially if the windows open to the south, so.uth-east, or sout li-weft, then it is very likely it will not keep long, but be muddy and stale : Therefore, to keep beer in such a cellar, it Ihould be brewed in October, that the drink may have time to oure itself before the hot weather comes on; but, in wettish or damp cellais, it is best to brew in March, that the drink may have time to fine and fettle before the winter weather is advanced. Now, cellars Ihould have double or treble doors, that the outer one may be shut before the inner one is opened, to keep the air out. If a cellar be kept dry, and have double doors, it is reckoned warm in winter, and cool in summer. But the best of celiais are thought to be those in chalks, . gravels, or

fands; and particularly in chalks, which are of a drying quality more. than any other, and ccufequently dissipate damps ; which contributes much to the gook keeping of the drink, for all damp cellars are prejudicial to the preservation of beers and ales, and sooner bring on the rotting of the calks and hoops than the dry ones. Besides, in such inclosed cellars and temperate air, the beers and ales ripen more kindly, are better digested and softened, and drink smoother : But, when the temperature of the air in the cellar is unequal, the drink soon grows stale. Though malt-liquor be truly brewed, yet it is often spoiled in a bad cellar, that occasions such alternate fermentations as to make it thick and four, though it sometimes happens that after such changes it fines itself again.’ To prevent these commotions of the beer, some brew their pale malt in March, and their brown in October ; because the pale malt, having not so many fiery particles in it as the brown, Hands more in need of the summer is weather to ripen it, while the brown fort, being more hard and dry, is better able to defend itself against the winter-colds that will help to smooth its harsh particles ; yet, when they happen to be too Violent, horse-duttg Ihould be laid to the windows as a fortification against them.

Some are of pinion, that Oftober is the best of all other months to brew any sort of malt in, by reason there are so many cold months directly following, that will digest the drink and make it much excel that brewed in March, because such beer will not want that care and watching, as that brewed in March absolutely requires, by often taking out and putting in the vent-peg on change of weather ; and, if it is always left out, then it deadens and palls the drink ; yet, if due care is not taken in this respect, a thunder or stormy night may marr all, by making the drink ferment and burst the ca/k ; for which rest on, as iron hoops are molt in fashion at this time, they are certainly the greatest security to the safety of the drink thus exposed ; and next to tliem is the chesnut-hoop ; both which will endure a Ihorter or longer time, as the cellar is more or lefs dry, and according to the management attending them : The iron hoops generally begin to ruft first at the edges, and therefore Ihould be rubbed off, and be kept from wet as much as possible.

Bricks are of great antiquity, as appears by the sacred writings, the tower and walls of Babylon being with them.

Pliny fays, that to make good bricks they must hot consist of any earth that is full of land or gravel, nor of such as is gritty or stony ; but of a grayish marl, or whitiflr chalky clay, or at lead of a reddish earth : He also adds, that the bell season for making bricks is the spring; because, ifmhde in summer, they will

Bricks, among us, are various, according to their various forms, dimenGons, tifes, method of making, &c. the principal of which are, Compass-bricks, of a circular form, used in fteyoiog of walls : Concave, or hollow bricks, on one side flat like a common brick, on the other hollowed, and used for conveyance of water : Feather-edged bricks, which are like common statute bricks, only thinner on one edge than the other, and used for penning up the brick pan ness in timber buildings : Cogging bricks are used for making the indented works under the caping of walls built with great bricks: Caping bricks, formed on purpose for caping of walls: Dutch or Flemish bricks, used to pave yards, stables, and for soap-boil ers vaults and cisterns : Clinkers, such brides as are glazed by the heat of the fire in making : Sandel or fames-bricks, are such as lie outmost in a kiln, or clamp, and consequently are soft and useless, as not being thoroughly burnt : Great bricks are those twelve inches long, six broad, and three thick, used to build fence-walls: Plailfer or buttress bricks, have a notch at one end, half the breadth of the brick ; their use is to bind the work which is built of great bricks : Statute-bricks or fern all common bricks, ought, when burnt, to be nine inches long, four and a quarter broad, and two and a half thick ; they arc commonly used in paving cellars, finks, hearths, <kc.

Bricks are burnt either in a kiln or clamp. Those that are burnt in a kiln, are Gift set or placed in it, and then the kiln being covered with pieces of bricks, they put in sonia wood to dry them with a gentle fire ; and this they continue till the bricks are pretty dry, which is known by the smoke’s turning from a darkish colour to a transparent smoke: They then leave off putting in wood, and proceed to make ready for burning, which is performed by putting in brush, furze, spray, heath, brake, or fern-faggots ; but before they put in any faggots, they dam up the mouth or mouths of the kiln with pieces of bricks (which they call Jhinlog ) piled up one upon another, and close it up with wet brick-earth, in lead of mortar.

The Ihinlog they make so high, that there is but just room above it to thrust in a faggot; then they proceed to put in more faggots, till the kiln and its arches look white, and the fire appears at the top of the kiln ; upon which they slacken the fire for an hour, and let all cool by degrees. This they continue to do, alternately heating and slacking, till the ware be, thoroughly burnt, which is usuaily effected in fortyeight hours.

About London they chiefly burn in clamps, built of the bricks themselves, after the manner of arches in kilns, with a vacancy between each brick, for the fire to play through ; but with this difference, that instead Of arching, they span it over by making the bricks project one over another on both (ides of the place, for. the wood and coals to lie in till they meet, and are bounded by the bricks at the top, which close all up.

The place for the fuel is carried up strait on both fides, till about three feet high ; then they almost fill it with wood, and over that lay a covering of sea-coal, and then overspan the arch; but they strew sea coal also over the clamp, betwixt all the rows of bricks ; laftly, they kindle the wood, which gives fire to the coal ; and when all is burnt, then they conclude the bricks are sufficiently burnt.

Oil of Bricks, olive oil imbibed by the substance of bricks, and afterwards distilled from it. This oil was once in great repute for curing many diseases, but is now entirely laid aside.-

bricking.c: BRICKING, among builders, the counterfeiting of a brick-wall on plkfter, which is done by smearing it over with red ochre, and making the joints with an edged tool ; these last are afterwards filled with a fine plaster.

bride.c: BRIDE, a woman newly married. Among the Greeks it was customary for the bride to be conduded from her father’s house to her husband’s in. a chariot, the evening being chosen for that puipofe, to conceal her blushes; fhe was placed in the middle, her husband fitting on one side, and one of her molt intimate friends on the other ; torches were carried before her, and flie was entertained in the passage with a song suitable to the occasion. When they arrived at their journey’s end, the axle-tree of the coach they rode in was burnt, to fig oily that the bride was never to return to her father’s house. Among the Romans, when a bride was carried home to her husband’s house, flie was not to touch the threshold at her first entrance, but was to leap over it.

bridegroom.c:
BRIDEGROOM, a man newly married, the spouse of the bride.

The Spartan bridegrooms committed a kind of rape upon their brides ; for matters being agreed on between them two, the woman that contrived and managed the match, having shaved the bride’s hair close to her Ikin, dressed her up in man’s cloaths, and left her upon a mattress ; this done, in came the bridegroom, in his usual dress, having supped as ordinary, and Healing as privately as he could to the room where the bride lay, and untying her virgin-girdle, took her to his embraces; and having flayed a Ihort time with her, returned to his companions, with whom he continued to.spend his life, remaining with them .by night as well as by day, unless he Hole a Ihort visit to his bride, which could not be done without a great deal of circumfpeaion, and fear of being difeevered.

bridewell.c:
BRIDEWELL, a work-house, or place of correction for vagrants, strumpets, and other disorderly persons.

These are made to work, being maintained with cl oa thing and diet ; and when it seems good to their governors, they are sent by pafies into their native countries : however, while they remain here, they are not only made to work, but, according to chcir crimes, receive, once a-for ting.ht, such a number of stripes as the governor commands. Yet to this hospital feveral hopeful and ingenious lads are put apprentices, and prove afterwards honest.and substantial citizens.

bridge.c:
BRIDGE, a work of masonry or timber, consisting of

one

B R I ( <

ene or more arches, built over a river, canal, or the like, for the conveniency of crossing the same.

Bridges are a sort of edifices very difficult to execute, on account of the inconvenience of laying foundations, and walling under water. The parts of a bridge are the piers, the arches ; the pavement, or way ever for cattle and carriages ; the foot-way on each side*, for foot passengers ; the rail or parapet, which incloses the whole ; and the butments or ends of the bridge on the bank.

The conditions required in a bridge are, that it be well-designed, commodious, durable, and suitably decorated. The piers of stone-bridges fliould be equal in number, that there may be one arch in the middle, where commonly the current is strongest ; their thickness is not to be lefs than a sixth part of the span of the arch, nor more than a fourth ; they are commonly guarded in the front with angular sterlings, to break the force of the current : the strongest arches are those whose sweep is a whole semicircle ; . as the piers of bridges always diminish the bed of a river, in cafe of inundations, the bed must be funk or hollowed in proportion to the space taken up by the piers (as the waters gain in depth what they lose in breadth) which otherwise conduce to wash away the foundation and endanger the piers : To prevent this, they sometimes diminish the current, either by lengthening its course, or by making it more winding ; or by flopping the bottom with rows of planks, flakes, or piles, which break the current. It is also required that thq foundation of bridges be laid at that season of the year, when the waters are lowest; and if the ground be rocky, hard gravel, or stony, the first stones of the foundation may be laid on the surface *, but if the foil be soft fand, it will be necessary to dig till you come to a firm bottom.

Among the bridges of antiquity, that built by Tfajan over the Danube is allowed to be the mod magnificent ; it was composed of twenty arches, of an hundred and fifty feet in height, and their opening from one pier to another was an hundred and sixty feet : The piers of this fine bridge are still to be seen in the Danube, being erected between Servia and Moldavia', a little above Nicopolis.

Among modern bridges, that of Westminster, built over the river Thames, may be accounted pne of the finest in the world : It is forty-four feet wide, a commodious foot-way being allowed for pafTengers, on each side, of about seven feet broad, raised above the ro^d allowed for carriages, and paved with broad moor-stones, while the space left between them is sufficient to 'admit three carriages and two horses to go a-breast, without any danger. Its extent from wharf to wharf is 1220 or 1223 feet, being full three hundred feet longer than. London-bride. The free water-way under the arches of this bridge is eight hundred and seventy feet, being four times as much as the free water-way left between the sterlings of Lon don-bridge: This disposition, together with the gen-' tleness of the stream, are the chief reasons why no sensible fall of water can ever flop, or in the least Vol. I. endanger the smallest boats in their pastage through the arches.

It consists of thirteen large and two small arches, together with fourteen intermediate piers.

Each pier terminates with a saliant right angle against either stream : the two middle piers are each seventeen feet in thickness at the (winging of the arches, and contain three thousand cubic feet, or near two hundred tons of solid stone ; and the others decrease in width equally on each side by one foot.

All the arches of this bridge are semicircular ; they all spring from about two feet above low-water mark; the middle arch is seventy-six feet wide, and the others decrease in breadth equally on each side by four feet.

This bridge is built of the best materials ; and the size and disposition of these materials are such, that there is no false bearing, or so much as a false joint in the whole structure ; besides that, it is built in a neat and elegant taste, and with such simplicity and grandeur, that, whether viewed from the water, or by the passengers who walk over it, it fills the mind with an agreeable fur prize. The femioftangular towers, which form the recedes of the foot-way, the manner of placing the lamps, and the height of the balustrade, are at once the most beautiful, and, in every other respect, the best contrived.

But the most Angular bridge in Europe is that built over the river Tave in Glamorganshire. It consists of one ftupenduous arch, the diameter of which is 175 feet, the chord 140, the altitude 39, and the abutments 32. This magnificent arch was built by William Edward, a poor coin try-mason, in the year 17S6Bridges are either built of stone or timber, as is judged most convenient.

StoneBridges consist of piers, arches, and butments, made of hewn stone, sometimes also intermixed with bricks.

WoodenBridges are composed of beams and joists, supported by punch sons, well cramped and bound together.

RujhenBridges are made of great bundles of rushes, bound fast together, over which planks are laid, and fattened : these are put Over marshy places, to serve for a crossing ground.

Pendent or hangingBridges, called also philosophical bridges, are those not supported by posts Or pillars, but hung at large in the air, sustained only at the two ends or butments.

Draw-B ridge, one that is fattened with hinges at one end only, so that the other may be drawn up ; in which cafe, the bridge stands upright, to hinder the passage of a ditch or moat.

Plying or floating Bridge, is generally made of two small bridges, laid ene over the other in such a mar» ner, that the uppermost stretches and runs out, by help of certain cords, running through pullies placed along the fides of the under bridge, which push it forwards, till the end of it joins the place it is intended to be fixed on.

Bridge of loots, boats made of copper, and joined side by side, till they reach a-cross a river, which being covered with planks, are fattened with flakes or anchors.

Bridge of communication is that made over a river, by which two armies, or forts, which are separated by that river, have a free communifcation with one another.

Floating Bridge, a bridge made use of, in form of a work in fortification, called a redoubt, confiding of two boats, covered with planks, which are solidly framed, so as to bear either horse or cannon.

Bridge, in gunnery, the* two pieces of timber which go between the two transums of a gun-carriage, on which the bed refts.

Bridge, in music, a term for that part of a {hinged instrument over which the firings are stretched. The bridge of a violin is about one inch and a quarter high, and near an inch and a half long.

Bridge-town, the capital of the island of Barbadoes : Weft Ion. 56°, and North lat. 13°. It has commodious wharfs for unlading goods, also some forts and castles for the defence of the place.

Bridge-north, a borough-town of Shropshire, situated on the river Severn, about fifteen miles south-east of Shrewsbury : Weft Ion. 2° 30', and North lat. 52° 40'. It fends two members to parliament.

Bridgewater, a large borough -town of Somerfetfhire, situated near the mouth of the river Evil, in 30 Weft long, and 510 ij' North lat. It fends two members to parliament.

bridle.c:
BRIDLE, in the menage, a contrivance made of straps or thongs of leather and pieces of iron, in order to keep a horse in subjection and obedience.

The feveral parts of a bridle are the bit, or snaffle; the head-stall, or leathers from the top of the head to the rings of the bit ; the fillet, over the fore-head and under the fore-top j the throat-band, which buttons from the head-band under the throat ; the reins, or long thongs of leather that come from the rings of the bit, and being cast over the horse’s head, the rider holds them in his hand ; the nose band, going through loops at the back of the head-stall, and buckled under the cheeks; the trench; the cave fan; the martingal ; and the chaff-halter.

Bridles imported pay a duty of 4 s. 9 T^d. the dozen ; whereof 4 s. is repaid on exporting

them again : besides which they also pay 6 s. for every 20 s. value upon oath, without any drawback.

Bridle-hand is the horseman’s left hand, the right hand being the spear or sword hand.

To swallow the Bridle, is slid of a horse that has too wide a mouth,, and too small a bit-mouth.

bridon.c: BRIDON, or Snaffle, after the English fashion, is a very slender bit-mouth, without any branches. The English make much use of them, and scarcely use any {rue bridles except in the service of war. The French call them bridons,. by way of distinction from bridles.

bridport.c:
BRIDPORT, a borough and port-town of Dorsetshire, situated about ten miles weft of Dorchester ; W. long. 30, and N. lat. 50° 40'.

It fends two members to parliament.

brief.c:
BRIEF, in Scots law, a writ issued from the chancery, directed to any judge-ordinary, commanding and authoring that judge to call a jury to inquire into the cafe mentioned in the brief, and upon their verdict to pronounce sentence.

Apojlolical Briefs,' letters which the pope dispatches to princes, or other magistrates, relating to any public affair.

These briefs are distinguished from bulls, in regard the latter are more ample, and always written on parchment, and fealed with lead or green wax ; whereas briefs are very concise, written on paper, fealed with red wax, and with the feal of the fisherman, or St Peter in a boat.

brieg.c: BRIEG, a town of Silesia, about twenty miles southeast of Breflaw; E. long. 170 2o\ and N. lat. 50® 50 .

briennois.c: BRIENNOIS, the southern division of the duchy of Burgundy, in France.

brieux.c: BRIEUX, a port-town of Britany, in France, situated on the English channel, about thirty miles weft of St Malo; W. long. 20 5c/, and N. lat. 48° 40'.

brigade.c:
BRIGADE, in the military art, a party or division of a body of soldiers, whether horse or foot, under the command of a brigadier.

An army is divided into brigades of horse and brigades of foot : a brigade of horse is a body of eight or ten squadrons ; a brigade of foot consists of four, five, or six battalions.

The eldest brigade has the right of the first line, and the second the right of the second, and the two next take the left of the two lines, and the youngest Hand in the centre.

Brigade-major, is an officer appointed by the brigadier, to assist him in the management and ordering of his brigade.

brigadier.c:
BRIGADIER is the general officer who has the command of a brigade. The eldest. colonels are generally advanced to this poll. He that is upon duty is brigadier of the day. They march at the head of their own brigades, and are allowed a serjeant and ten men of their own brigade for their guard.

Brigadiers, and Sub-brigadiers, are polls in the horse-guards.

brigandine.c: BRIGANDINE, a coat of mail, a kind of ancient defensive armour, consisting of thin jointed scales of plate, pliant and easy to the body.

brigantine.c: BRIGANTINE, a small light vessel, which can both row and fail well, and is either for fighting or giving chaee. It hath about twelve or fifteen benches for the rowers, one man to a bench ; all the hands aboard are soldiers, and each man hath his musquet lying ready under his oar.

brigg.c: BRIGG, a market-town in Lincolnshire, about twentyfour miles north of Lincoln; W. long. 20', and N. lat. *3° 4°"-

brightelmstone.c: BRIGHTELMSTONE, a little port-town in Sufiex, about seven miles south-weft of Lewes ; W. long, \d , and N. lat. 5a0 50'.

BRIHUEGA, a town of New Castile, in Spain, about forty-three miles north-east of Madrid; W. long. 30 20',- and N. lat. 41°.

BRILL* or Brie l, the capital of the island of Voorn, in Holland, situated about twelve miles south of the Hague; E, long. 40, and N. lat. 51° 50'.

brilliant.c:
BRILLIANT, in a general sense, something that has a lucid and bright appearance.

Brilliant, in the menage, a brisk, high-mettled, slate ly horse, is called brilliant, as having a rai ed neck, a fine motion, excellent haunches, upon which he rifes, though never so little put on.

BRIM denotes the utmost verge or edge, especially of round things.

Brim, in country affairs. A sow is said to brim, or to go to brim, when fhe is ready to take boar.

BRIMSTONE. See Sulphur, and Chemistry.

Bri-mstone-wm*. . See Marble.

brin.c: BRIN, a city of Moravia, dependent on Bohemia, about thirty miles south-weft of Olmutz : E. long. 160 20', and N. lat. 490 40'.

brindisi.c: BRINDISI, a port-town of the kingdom of Naples, situated on the gulph of Venice, about thirty-five miles north-weft of Otranto; E. long. 180 45', andN. lat. 40° 40 .

brine.c:
BRINE, water replete with saline particles ; or pickle.

Brine-w^/ct, a fait water, which being boiled, turns into fait.

Brine taken out of brine-pits, or brine-pans, used by some for curing or pickling of fish, without boiling the same into fait, and rock-salt without refining it into white-salt, are prohibited by 1 Anne, cap. xxi.

BRINGING-IN a horse , in the menage, the same as to say, keep down the nose of a horse that boars, and tofles his nose in the wind ; this is done by means of a good branch. See Banquet, and Wind.

brion.c: BRION, an island of North America, in the gulph of St Lawrence.

briones.c: BRIONES, a small town of Old Castile, in Spain, situated on the river Ebro.

brioni.c: BRIONI, the name of three islands in the Adriatic sea, upon the western coast of Iftria. They belong to the Republic of Venice.

brionne.c: BRIONNE, a town of Normandy, in France, situated on the Rill, about ten leagues from Rouen.

brisac.c:
BRISAC, a fortified town-of Swabia, in Germany, situated on the eastern shore of the river Rhine, about thirty miles north of Strafburg; E. long. 70 1 j', and N. lat. 48° io'.

New Brisac, a fortress on the western shore of the Rhine, opposite to Old Brifac. It is situated in Ai face, and belongs to the French.

brisgow.c: BRISGOW, a territory of the circle of Swabia, in Germany, situated on the east side of the Rhine, opposite to the Upper Alface, whereof Fribourg and Bri fac are the chief towns.

bristle.c:
BRISTLE, a rigid glossy kind of hair, found on swine, and much used by brufhmakers, <bc.

Bristles, rough and undressed, pay aduty of is. 2ttoV1. dozen pound, whereof 1 s. -^5d, is drawn back on exporting them -, whereas dressed bristles pay a duty of 2 s. 4-^^d. the dozen pound, whereof 2 s, >s drawn back on exportation..

The whiskers of cats are also sometimes called bristles ; as are the quills of the porcupine.

bristol.c:
BRISTOL, a city and port-town of England, situated" partly in Gloucefterfhire, and partly in Somerfetfhire ; W. long. 20 40', and N. lat. 51 0 30'.

It stands on the river Avon, about ninety miles weft of London, and is a town of the greatest foreign trade of any in Britain next to London. It is also a bishop’s fee, fends two members to parliament, and gives the title of ear] to the noble family of Harvey.

New Bristol, the capital of the county of Bucks, in Penfilvania, about twenty miles north of Philadelphia. It is situated on the river Delawar, in 75 0 W. long, and 40° 45' N. lat.

Bristol water. These waters are the fourth in degree amongst the waters which are esteemed warm. The waters of Bath are the first, Buxton the second^ and Matlock the third.

Bath waters are beneficial, when the fecietions from’ the blood are diminished ; Bristol, when too much increased: Bath attenuates powerfully ; Bristol incrassates : Bath is spirituous, and helps defers ; Bristol is more cooling, and suppresses plentitude, with its’ consequences, inflammations and haemorrhages, *

If we may judge of the contents of Bristol waters, from their effects, which are exceedingly detersive and healing ; they partake chiefly of chalk, lapis calcarius, and calaminaris, the virtues of which are too dry to cleanse y they fill ulcers with fief st, and cicatrize them.

But whatever the substances are that impregnate them, it is plain they are very subtile, and that there is but little of a terrestrial part in them, from their specific lightness above other waters : Yet when we confider how agreeable to the fight,, smell and taste ; how clear, pure and soft they are ; their gentle degree of heat, so adapted to sundry diseases ; it must be concluded, that those waters do imbibe some salutary particles in their passage through the earth ; and, from; the many cures yearly wrought by them, that they have an undoubted tittle to a place in the first class of medicinal waters.

The diseases in which Bristol waters are properly prescribed, are internal haemorrhages and inflammations, blood-spitting, dysentery, and immoderate flux of the menses, purulent ulcers of the viscera : Hence, in consumptions, the dropsy, scurvy with heat, stone, gravel, strangury ; the habitual gput, scorbutic rheuraatifm, diabetes, flowfevers, atrophy, pox, cancer, gleets in both fexes, king’s evil, etc\ ; in all these disorders, Bath waters are not only improper, but hurtful ; they rouse the too languid, and quicken the too lazy circulation; they allay the heat, and restrain the too rapid motion of the blood. Those impregnate the phlegmatic, these attemperate the choleric constitution. Bath water seems to be adapted to the maladies of the stomach, guts, and nerves; Bristol, to those of the: lungs, kidneys, and bladder : Again, Bath waters are at variance with a milk course ; and the Bristol can never be judiciously diredled, but when they may be: joined with reason and success.

Bristol in botany, a name sometimes given to the lichnis. See Lichnis.

britain.c:
BRITAIN, or Gre at-britain, the mod considerabie of all the European islands, lies between yo° and 6o° N. lat. and between 20 E. long, and 6° W. long.

The general division of Britain, is into South and North Britain, or England and Scotland.

It is fubs del to Great-Britain, but yields only {kins and furs.

brite.c: BRITE, or Bright, in husbandry. Wheat, barley, or any other grain, is said to brite, when it grows 0ver ripe, and {hatters.

brittleness.c:
BRITTLENESS, that quality of bodies, on account of which they are denominated brittle, or which subjects them to be easily broken.

BRIVE la GAiLLA&bE, a town of France in the Limoufin, upon the Coureze.

brixen.c: BRIXEN, a city of Tyrol in Germany, about fifty miles north-east of Trent: E. long. 110 45', N. lat. 46° 45'.

briza.c: BRIZA, a genus of the triandria digynia class. There are five species of Briza, two of which are natives of Britain, viz. the media or middle quaking grafs, and the minor or small quaking-grafs. They grow in pasture-grounds.

brize.c:
BRIZE, in husbandry, denotes ground that has lain long untilled.

Brize-* tents, {helters used by gardeners who have not walls on the north-side, to keep cold winds from damaging their beds of melons. broadalbin.c:
BROAD ALBIN, a distri<St or county of Perthlhire, in Scotland, bordering upon Argyleshire : It gives the title of earl to a branch of the noble family of Campbell.

BROAD-^fisc, in the sea-language, denotes a volley of cannon, or a general discharge of all the guns on one side of a {hip at once.

brocade.c:
BROCADE, or Brocado, a fluff of gold, silver, or silk, raised and enriched with flowers, foliages, and

other ornaments, according to the fancy of the merchants or manufacturers.

Formerly the word figriified only a fluff, wove all of gold, both in the warp and in the woof, or all of silver, or of both mixed together ; thence it passed to those of fluffs in which their was silk mixed, to raise and terminate the gold or silver flowers : But at present all fluffs, even those of silk alone, whether they be grograms of Tours or of Naples, fattins, and even taffeties or lustrings, if they be but adorned and worked with some flowers, or other figures, are called brocades.

Brocade-^*?//, the English name of a species of limax. See Limax.

brocatel.c: BROCATEL, or Brocadel, a kind of coarse brocade; chiefly used for tapestry.

broccoli.c:
BROCCOLI, a kind of cabbage cultivated for the use of the table; the manner of dressing which is this: When their heads are gfown to their full bigness, they are to be cut off, with about four inches of the tender stem ; the outer fitin is then to be stripped off the stem, after which they are to be washed, and boiled in a clean sinner cloth, as is pradtifed for cauliflowers.

They are tenderer than any cauliflower, though very like them in taste.

brock.c:
BROCK, among sportsmen, a term used to denote a badger.

A hart too of the third year is called a brock, or brocket ; and a hind of the. same year, a brocket’s filter.

brod.c: BROD, a town of Sclavonia, situated on the river Save, about sixteen miles south of Pofega : E.long. 180 50', N. lat. 45 9 2C3 .

brodera.c: BRODERA, or Brodra, a city of Alia, in the country of the Mogul and kingdom of Guzurat, where there is a great trade in cotton cloths : E. long. 73° 30', N. lat. 22° 25'.

brodium.c:
BRODIUM, a pharmaceutical term, signifying the same as ju scutum, or the liquor in which some solid medicine is preserved, or with which something elfe is diluted.

BROGLING for eels , the same with snigg ling. See Sniggling.

broglio.c:
BROGLIO, a town of Peidmont in Italy, situated near the frontiers of Provence, about twenty five miles north-weft of Nice : E. long. 6° 42', N. lat. 44° i2/.

It is the capital of a county of the same name.

broitschia.c:
BROITSCHIA, a city of Asia in Indoftan, about twelve leagues from Surat.

BROKEN •wind, 'kmong farriers, is a malady that happens to a horse when he is suffered to stand too long in the liable, without exercise : By this means he contrails gross and thick humours in such abundance, that, adhering to the hollow parts of his lungs, they flop his wind-pipe.

This distemper is known by the horse’s heaving and drawing up his flanks together, and blowing wide his nostrils.

To cure this disorder, take the guts of a hedge hog, dry

dry them, and pound them to powder, and give the horse two or three spoonfuls of it in a pint of wine or strong ale ; then mix the reft with anise-feed, liquorice, and sweet butter, of which make round balls, or pills, and give him two or there of them after drink, and let him fall two or three hours.

broker.c:
BROKER, a name given to persons of feveral and very different professions, the chief of which are exchangebrokers, stock-brokers, pawn brokers, and brokers, limply so called, who fell household-furniture, and second-hand apparel. V

ExchangeBrokers are a kind of agents, or negotiators, who contrive, propose, and conclude bargains between merchants, and between merchants and tradesmen, in matters of bills of exchange, or merchandise, for which they have so much commission. These, by the statute of 8 and 9 William III. are to be licensed in London by the Lord Mayor, who gives them an oath, and takes bond for the faithful execution of their offices. If any person shall a<5t as broker, without being thus licensed and admitted, he shall forfeit the sum of jpol. and persons employing him j 1. and brokers are to register contrails, &>c. under the like penalty: Alfo brokers shall not deal for themselves, on pain of forfeiting 200 1. They are to carry about with them a silver medal, having the king’s arms, and the arms of the city, and pay 40s. a year to the chamber of the city.

The exchange brokers make it their business to know the alteration of the course of exchange, to inform merchants how it goes, and to give notice to those who have money to receive or pay beyond sea ; they -are the proper persons for negotiating the exchange, and when the matter is accomplished, that is, when the money for the bill is paid, and the bill delivered, they have for brokerage 2 s. for iool. sterling.

They reckon at Paris, among the city-officers, who are employed under the jurisdiction of the provost of the merchants, and echevins or aldermen, three forts of brokers.

1 . The brokers of horses for the carriage of merchandise by water ; they are established for the navigation, and take care to examine the horses used to draw the boats up the river ; to set the horses together, to oblige the carriers to repair their boats, or to break such as are no longer fit to serve.

2. Sworn wine-brokers on the keys, to examine and taste all the wine that arrives there.

3. Brokers of bacon and lard. These are established to examine those forts of merchandises, as they are landed or unloaded, and to answer for their goodness to the buyer, and to the feller, for the price of his wares.

5/ccLBrokers, are those who are employed to buy and fell shares in the joint stock of a company, or corporation.

Panun-Bv. oxers. Persons who keep (hops, and lend money upon pledges to necessitous persons, and mod commonly at an exorbitant interest. They are more properly styled pawn-takers, or tally men, sometimes strip ers, orfriperers. These are meant in 1 Jac.I. cap. xxi. sect. 5. where it is declared, that the sale of goods wrongfully taken to any broker, or pawn-broker in London, Westminster, Southwark, or within two miles of London, does not alter the property.

And sect. 7. If a broker, having received such goods, shall not, upon request of the owner, discover them, how and when he came by them, ar,d to whom they are conveyed, he fi all forfeit the double value thereof, to be recovered by at tion of debt, icy.

In the cities of Italy, there are companies established by authority for the letting out money on pawns, called mounts of piety ; a title little becoming such ioftitutions, as the loan is not gratis. In some parts of Italy, they have alio mounts of piety of another kind, wherein they only receive ready money, and return it again with interest, at a certain sum per annum .

At Bologna, they have feveral such mounts, which are distinguished into frank and perpetual ; the interest of the former is only four per cent . that of the latter, seven.

Brokers are also those who fell old household-furniture, and wearing apparel, icy.

bromelia.c: BROMELIA, or pine apple, in botany, a genus of the hexandria monogynia class. The calix is divided into three segments ; it has three petals, and there is a scaly nedlarium at the base of each petal ; the berry has three ceils. There are five species of bromelia, viz. the ananas or common pine-apple, which is .a native of Surinam and New Spain ; the ping un, a native of Jamaica and Barbadoes ; the karatos, lingulata, and nudicaulis, all natives of the southern parts of America.

bromsgrove.c: BROMSGROVE, a market-town in Worcestershire, about ten miles north of Worcester : W. long. 20 N. lat. 520 26'.

bromley.c:
BROMLEY, a market-town of Kent, ten miles southeast of London: E. long. 5', N. lat. 510 2 j\

Bromley is also the name of a markettown of Staffordshire, about ten miles east of Stafford : W. long. 1° jo', N. lat. 520 45'.

BROMOIDES, in botany. See Festtjca.

bromus.c: BROMUS, in botany, a genus of the triandria digynia class. The calix is double-valved ; the spica is oblong and cylindrical ; the awn is below the apex. There are 17 species, eight of which are natives of Britain, viz. the fecalinus or field brome-grals, the arvensis or corn brome grafs, the ciliatus or wall brome-grafs, the sterilis or barren brome-grafs, the giganteus or tall brome-grafs, the ramosus or wood brome grafs, and the pinnatus or spiked brome-grafs.

bronchia.c: BRONCHIA, in anatomy, the ramifications -of the trachea. See p. 280. (col. 2.) & p. 281.

bronchocele.c:
BRONCHOCELE, in surgery, a tumour arising in the anterior part cf the neck. See Surgery.

bronchotomy.c: BRONCHOTOMY, in surgery, an incision made in the aspera arteria, or windpipe, which is necessary in many cafes, and especially in a violent quinsey, to prevent suffocation from the great inflammation or tumor of the parts. It is also called laryngotomy and tracheotomy. See Surgery.

bronchus.c:
BRONCHUS, according to Galen, is the aspera arteria which reaches from the larynx to the lungs, confiding of the bronchia.

Sometimes it is put for the whole aspera arteria; and Hippocrates nfes it to signify the throat.

BRONTIAT., or Thunder:stones, in natural hide ry. See Belemnites.

brontium.c:
BRONTIUM, in Grecian antiquity, a place underneath the floor of the theatres, in which were kept brazen vessels full of dories and other materials, with which they imitated the noise of thunder.

BRONTOLOGY denotes the dod trine of thunder, or an explanation of its caufes, phaenomena, <&c. together with the presages drawn from it. See Thunder, and Electricity.

bronze.c: BRONZE, a compound metal, confiding of one part of tin, ten of copper, and a little zinei See Chemi str y.

bronzes.c:
BRONZES, a name given by antiquarians to figures either of then or beads, to urns, and, in general, to every piece of sculpture which the ancients made of that metal. We likewise give the name of bronzes to datues or buds cad of bronze, whether these pieces be copies of antiques, or original fubjedls.

Among medallids, all copper medals bear the name of bronze.

bronzing.c:
BRONZING, the art of varnidiing Wood, plader, ivory, .etc. so as to give them the colour of bronze. See Varnishing.

BROOD, the young of fish, fowls, &c.

brooding.c:
BROODING, the adl of a hen in hatching her eggs.

BROOK, a little river or small current of water.

A brook is didinguifhed from a river insomuch as a river flows at all times, whereas a brook flows at some particular seasons. only.

Brook “lime. See Anagallis.

BROOM, in botany. See Genista.

Broom-flower, ordre de la ger.isle, an order instituted by St Louis, king of France, to flew the esteem which he bad for the queen his wife, who, the.evening before his queen’s coronation, received this order himself.

Broom-rape, in botany. See Orobanche.

brooming.c:
BROOMING, or Breaming, of a Jhip, the wall ting and burning off all the filth that {he has contra&ed on her fides with weeds, draw, broom, or the like, when die is on the careen, or on the ground. See Cap.eening.

BROTHEL. See Stews.

brother.c:
BROTHER, a term of relation between male children, spi sung from the same parents, or from the same lathe4,' or the same mother.

The ancients used the term brother, indifferently, to almost all who stood related in the collateral line, as uncles and nephews, cousins-german, &c.

According to the laws of Mofes, the brother of a man, who died without children, was obliged to marry the widow of the deceased, in order to raise up children to him, that his name and memory might not be ex tind. See the article Widow.

Among us, it is cudomary for kings to give the title brother to each other.

In the civil law, brothers, fratres, in the plural number, sometimes comprehends fiders.

Brother is also a customary term for prieds of the same persuasion to address one another by ; but it is more particularly used to denote the relation between monks of the same convent, as father Zachary : In English, we more usually say, Friar Zachary, from the French word frere, brother. Preachers also call their hearers, my brethren, or my dear brethren ; and sometimes they use the singular number, and lay, my brother.

This appellation is borrowed, from the primitive Chridians, who all called each other brothers: but it is now principally used for such of the religious as are not prieds ; those in orders are generally honoured with the title of father, whereas the reft are only simply brothers.

Brotkers-german. See German.

Brothers of the rosy-cross. See Ro si crucian.

brouck.c: BROUCK, the name of a town of Germany, in the circle of Wedphalia, upon the river Roer ; and likewise of a town of Switzerland, upon the banks of the Aar.

brouershaven.c: BROUERSHAVEN, a port-town of Zeland, in the united Netherlands, situated on the north side of the island of Schonen, about nine miles south-wed of Helvoetfluys: E. Ion. -f 55', and N. 1 at . - 5 1 0 50'.

brow.c:
BROW, or Eye-brow, an hairy arch extended over the orbit of each eye. See p, 291. col. 1.

BROW-post, among builders, denotes a beam which goes across a budding.

Brow-antler, among sportsmen, that branch of a deer’s horn next the tail.

browallia.c: BROWALLIA, in botany, a genus of the didynamia angiospermia class. The calix has five teeth ; the limbus of the corolla is divided into five equal and open segments ; and the capsule is unilocular.

brown.c:
BROWN, among dyers, painters, &c. a dust try colour^ inclining towards redness. Of this colour there are various {hades or degrees, didinguiflied by different appellations ; for indance, Spanidiforown, a fad brown,. a town ey-brown, the London brown, a clove brown, <&c.

Spanifti-brown is a dark dull red, of a horse-flesh colour. It is an earth, and is of great use among painters, being generally used as the first and priming colour that they lay upon any kind of timberwork in house painting. That which is of the deeped colour, and freed from stones, is the bed. Though this is of a dirty brown colour, yet it is much used, not to colour any garment, unltfs it be an old man’s gown;

gown ; but to shadow ver million, or to lay upon any dark ground behind a pi&.ure, or to shadow yellow berries in the darkest places, when you want lake, be. It is bell and bright ell when burnt in the fire, till it be red hot, although, if you would colour any hare, horse, dog, or the like, it Ihould not be burnt; but, for other ufes, it is bell when it is burnt ; as for instance, for colouring wood, ports, bodies of trees, or any thing elfe of wood, or any dark ground of a pi&ure. See Dying.

brownists.c: BROWNISTS, in church-history, a religious fed, which sprung up in England towards the end of the XVIth century. Their leader was one Robert Brown, born at Northampton. They separated from the established church, on account of its discipline and form of government. They equally disliked episcopacy and presbyterianism. They condemned the solemn celebration of marriages in churches, maintaining, that matrimony being a political contract, the. confirmation of it ought to proceed from the civil magistrate. They rese&ed all forms of prayer, and held, that the Lord’s prayer was not to be recited as a prayer; being given only as a model, upon which to form our prayers.

bruchsal.c: BRUCHSAL, a town of the bishopric of Spires, in the palatinate of the Rhine, in Germany : E. Ion. 8° 30', and N. lat. 49® 15'.

bruchus.c: BRUCHUS, in zoology, a genus of infeds belonging to the order of caleoptera. The feelers are filiform, and gradually increase in thickness. There are seven species, viz. the pifi, has grey elytra interspersed with white spots, and a white fundament with two black spots. The theolromae with whitish elytra interspersed with black points. It frequents the theolroma or chocolate trees in the East Indies. 3.' The badris, with smooth elytra, a hoary body, and’ the hind part of*the thighs oval. If frequents the palm-trees of Jamaica. 5. The granarius, has black elytra; the fore feet are red, and the hind-feet are dentated. It frequents the feeds of plants in different parts of Europe. 6. The femiparius is black, with the base of the feelers and fore-feet testaceous. It is about the size of a loufe, and a native of Europe. 7. The ptdicornis, with comb-shaped feelers longer than the body. It is a native of Barbary and China.

bruges.c:
BRUGES, a city and port-town of Flanders, eleven miles east of Ostend, and twenty-four northwest of Ghent: E. Ion. 30 5', and N. lat. 51° 16'.

brumalia.c:
BRUMALIA, in Roman antiquity, festivals of Bacchus celebrated twice a-year; the first on the twelfth of the calends of March, and the other on the eighteenth of the calends of November. They were mftituted by Romulus, who, during these feasts, used to entertain the senate. Among other heathen festivals which the primitive Christians were much inclined to observe, Tertullian mentions the brumas or brumalia.

BRUNELLA, in botany. See Prunella.

brunia.c: BRUNIA, in botany, a genus of the pentandria monogynia class. The dowers are aggregated ; the filaments of the llamina are inferred into the ungues of the petals ; the stigma is bifid, and the feeds are fmgle. There are six species, all natives of iEtlnopta.

brunsbuttel.c: BRUNSBUTTEL, a port-town of Holstein, in the circle of Lower Saxony, in Germany, situated at the mouth of the river Elbe : E. Ion. 8° 42^ and N. lat. 540 io/. It is fubjed to Denmark.

brunsfelsia.c: BRUNSFELSIA, in botany, a genus of the penfandria monogynia class. The corolla is long and shaped like a tunnel ; the berry is unilocular, and contains many feeds.

brunswick.c:
BRUNSWICK, the capital of the duchy of Brunswick, in the circle of Lower Saxony, in Germany, situated on the river Ocker, about 35 miles east of Hanover : E. Ion. io° 30V and N lat. 52® 3c/.

, The ele&or of Hanover is styled duke of Brunswick', though he has no property in, or dominion over, the city of that name, which belongs to the duke of Brunswick Wolfembuttle.

In the choice of painters bruflres, observe whether the bristles are fast bound in the stocks, and if the hair be strong and lie close together ; for if they sprawl abroad, sueh will never work well ; and if they are not fast bound in the flock, the bristles will come out when you are using them, and spoil your work, as may be seen where the loose hairs of the brush have lain up and down in the colours laid on, to the great detriment of the work.

Wine-brushes are of use for se rubbing those silver, .

• copper, and brass pieces, which are to be gilded over, in order ta clear them perfectly from any dirt, ruft, or filth, which may adhere to them, and, if not brushed off, would hinder the doling of the gold with them. They are therefore used by gilders, silversmiths, be. and are usually sold by ironmongers. Beard-bruflies pay a duty, on importation, of 1 s. 3-/./^. the gross or twelve dozen; whereof is.. 14 is drawn back on exporting them. brussels.c:
BRUSSELS, the capital of the province of Brabant, and of all the Austrian Netherlands. It is situated on the river Senne, and is the fee of a bishop; W. long. 40 6', and N. lat. 50° jo'.

It is a strong fortified town, and agreeably situated, which, together with the viceroy’s residence, occasions a great resort of nobility and gentry.

brute.c: BRUTE, an animal guided moltly by mere instinct, and comprehends all animals, excepting mankind.

bruton.c: BRUTON, a market-town in Somerfetlhire, about ten miles south-east of Wells; W. long. 20 35', and N. lat. Ji° ij'.

bryansbridge.c: BRYANSBRIDGE, a town of Ireland, in the county of Clare, and province of Connaught, situated on the river Shannon, about eight miles north of Limerick.

brygmus.c: BRYGMUS, among physicians, a grating noise made by the gnashing of teeth.

bryonia.c:
BRYONIA, in botany, a genus of the monoecia syngenesia class. The calix of the male has five teeth ; the corolla is divided into five segments ; and there are three filaments. The calix of the female is likewise teethed ; the corolla has five divisions ; the stylus is trifid ; and the berry is roundish, and contains many feeds. There are six species of bryony, only one of which, viz. the alba, or white bryony, is a native of Britain. The root is a strong cathartic, and, applied externally, is said to be a powerful discutient.

Black bryony. See Tamus.

bryum.c: BRYUM, in botany, a genus of the cryptogamia musci class. The anthera is covered with an operculum ; the calyptra is smooth. There are 41 species, moll of them natives of Britain.

bubalis.c: BUBALIS, in zoology, the trivial name of the buffalo, a species of the bos. See Bos.

bubble.c:
BUBBLE, in philosophy, small drops or vesicles of any fluid filled with air, and either formed on its surface, by an addition of more of the fluid, as in raining, C 'zc. ; or in its substance, by an intestine motion of its component particles. Bubbles are dilatable or compressable, i. e. they take up more or lefs room, as the included air is more or lefs heated, or more or lefs pressed from without, and are round, because the included air ads equally from within, all around.

Bubble, in commerce, a cant term given to a kind of pro sed for raising of money on imaginary grounds, much pradifed in France and England in the years 1719, 1720, and 1721.

The pretence of those schemes was the raising a capital for retrieving, fetting on foot, or carrying on some promising and useful branch of trade, manufacture, machinery, or the like : To this end proposals were made out, shewing the advantages to be derived from the undertaking, and inviting persons to be engaged in it. The sum necessary to manage the affair, together with the profits expeded from it, were divided into shares or subscriptions, to be purchased by any disposed to adventure therein.

Bubbles, by which the public have been tricked.

are of two kinds, viz. 1. Those which we may properly enough term trading-bubbles ; and, 2. Stock or fund-bubbles. The former have been of various kinds ; and the latter at different times, as in 1719 and 1720.

bubo.c:
BUBO, in ornithology, the trivial name of a species of strix. See Strix.

Bubo, or Buboe, in surgery, a tumour which arises, with inflammation, only in certain or particular parts to which they are proper, as in the arm-pits and in the groins. See Medicine, and Surgery.

bubon.c: BUBON, in botany, a genus of the pentandria digynia class. The fruit is oval, striated, and hairy. There are four species, and none of them natives of Britain.

bubonocele.c:
BUBONOCELE, or Hernia inguinalis, in surgery, a tumour in the inguen, formed by a prolapsus of the intestines, omentum, or both, through the processes of the peritonaeum, and rings of the abdominal muscles. See Surgery.

BUBONIUfyl, in botany, a fynonime of the inula. See Inula.

bucanephyllon.c: BUCANEPHYLLON, in botany, the name by which PI ukenet calls the farracena. See Sarracena.

bucardia.c: BUCARDIA, or Bucarditje, in natural history, a kind of figured (tones, formed in the cavities of the larger cock les, and resembling, in some measure, a heart at cards.

bucariza.c:
BUCARIZA, a town of the kingdom of Hungary, in Croatia, upon the Adriatic sea, in a gulf that takes the same name.

BUCCA ferrea , in botany, a name given by Micheli to the ruppia of Linnaeus. See Ruppia.

buccal.c: BUCCAL, something belonging to the cheeks : Thus, the buccal glands, are those dispersed over the inner side of the cheeks.

buccaneers.c:
BUCCANEERS, those who dry and smoke flesh or fish, after the manner of the Americans.

This name is particularly given to the French inhabitants of the island of St Domingo, whose whole employment is to hunt bulls, or wild boars, in order to fell the hides of the former, and the flesh of the latter.

The buccaneers are of two forts : The buccaneers ox-hunters, or rather hunters of bulls and cows ; and the buccaneers boar-hunters, who are Amply called hunters ; though it seems, that such a name be lefs proper to them than the former ; since the latter smoke and dry the flesh of wild boars, which is properly called buccaneering, whereas the former prepare only the hides, which is done without buccaneering.

Buccaneering is a term taken from Buccan, the place where they smoke their flesh or fish, after the manner of the savages, on a grate or hurdle, made of Brasil wood, placed in the smoke, a confiderable distance from the fire : This place is a hut, of about twenty five or thirty feet in circumference, all surrounded and covered with palmetto leaves.

Buccaneers also signify those famous adventurers of all the nations in Europe, who join together to make war again II the Spaniardsof America, cruising about in privateers, to take all the vessels and small craft they can meet with.

BUCCARI,

Buccari, or Bouchari, is also the name of a large province of Asiatic Tartary, situated between 78° and

yo° E. Ion. and 340 and 440 N. lat.

buccellarii.c: BUCCELLARII, an order of soldiery under the Greek emperors, appointed to guard and distribute the ammunition-bread ; though authors are somewhat divided as to their office and quality. Among the Visigoths, buccellarius was a general name for a client or vassal who lived at the expence of his lord. Some give the denomination to parasites in the courts of piinces, some make them the body-guards of empeiors, and some fancy they were only such as emperors employed in putting persons to death privately.

buccina.c: BUCCINA, an ancient musical and military instrument. It is usually taken for a kind of trumpet ; which opinion is confirmed by Festus, by his defining it a crooked horn, played on like a trumpet. Vegetius observes, that the buccina bent in a semicircle, in which refpeA it differed from the tuba or trumpet. It is very hard to distinguish it from the cornu or horn, unless it was something !efs, and not quite so crooked; yet it certainly was of a different species, because we never read of the cornu in use with the watch, but only the buccina. Besides, the found of the buccina was (harper, and to be heard much farther, than either the cornu or the tuba. In scripture, the like instrument, used both in war and in the temple, was called ramshorns, kiren-jobes, and fopheroth hagijcbelim.

buccinum.c: BUCCINUM or Trumpet-shell, a genus of (hell fish belonging to the order of vermes tettacese. This animal is one of the snail kind. The (hell is univalve, spiral, and gibbous. The aperture is oval, ending in a small strait canal. Linnaeus enumerates about sixty species, moil of which are found in the southern seas.

bucco.c: BUCCO, in ornithology, a genus belonging to the order of picx. The beak is cultrated, turned inwards, compressed on the Tides, and emarginated on each side at the apex ; and there is a long (lit below the eyes. The nostrils are covered with feathers. The feet have four toes, two before and two behind. There is but one species, viz. the capensis, which is of a reddiffi colour, with a yellow belt round the (shoulders, and a black one round the br eft. It is found at the Cape of Good-Hope.

buccula.c: BUCCULA, in antiquity, denotes the umbo, or moil prominent part in the middle of a (held ; so called, because usually fashioned like the mouth or face of a man or other animal.

bucentaur.c:
BU CENTAUR, a galeas, or large galley of the doge of Venice, adorned with line pillars on both (ides, and gilt over from the prow to the stern. This vessel is covered over head with a kind of tent, made of purple silk. In it the doge receives the great lords and persons of quality that go to Venice, accompanied with the ambassadors and counsellors of (late, and all the Senators Seated on benches by him. The same vessel Serves also in the magnificent ceremony of ascension vol. I. No. 29. 3

day, on which the Duke of Venice throws a ring into the sea to espouse it, and to denote his dominion over the gulph of Venice.

Bucentaur is also the name of a (hip, as great and s magnificent as that of the Venetians, built by order of the elector of Bavaria, and launched on a lake, which is six leagues in length.

buceros.c: BUCEROS, in ornithology, a genus belonging to the order of picae. The beak is convex, cultrated, very large, and Serrated outwards : The fore-head is naked, with a bony gibbosity, The nostrils are behind the base of the beak. The tongue is (harp and (short. The feet are of the graffarii kind, i. e. the toes are distinct from each other. There are four species of the buceros, viz. 1. The bicornis, with a flat bony fore-head, and two horns before. The body is black, and about the size of a hen ; but the breast, belly and thighs are white. There is a white spot on the wing ; the tail is long, with ten black prime feathers, and the four outermost on each are white. The feet are greenifti, with three toes before and one behind. It is a native of China, and called Calao by Willoughby and other authors. 2. The hydroccrax, or Indian crow of Ray, has a plain bony fore-head without any horns. The body is yellowiffi, and black - illi below. It inhabits the Molucca isles. 3. The rhinoceros, has a crooked horn in the fore-head joined to the upper mandible. It is a native of India, and feeds upon carrion. 4. The nafutus, has a fin oath fore-head. It is about the size of a magpie, and is a native of Senegal.

buchan.c: BUCHAN, a country or district of Aberdeenihire, in Scotland : It gives the title of Earl, to the noble and ancient family of Erskine.

bucharest.c: BUCHAREST, a town of Wallachia, subjest to the Turks : E. Iob. 26° 30', and N. lat. 440 20'.

buchorn.c: BUCHORN, a city of Swabia, in Germany, situated on the east side of the lake of Conftance, and about twelve miles east of the city of Conftance : E. long. 9° 20', and N. lat. 47 0 40'.
