The fasti ion or form of buckles is various ; but their use, in general, is to make fast certain parts of dress, as the (hoes, garters, <&c.

Buckles for girdles pay a duty of 3 s. ioTVtj-d. the gross, or twelve dozen; whereof is. 44 st. is drawn back on exportation. Buckles for girts pay likewise a duty of is. fi^d. the gross; and both these pay sinew hat more, if of brass. But it is be observed, that all buckles are prohibited to be imported.

buckler.c:
BUCKLER, a piece of defensive armour used by the ancients. It was worn on the left arm, and composed of wickers woven together, or wood of the lightest fort, but most commonly of hides, fortified with plates of brass ot metal. The figure was sometimes round, sometimes oval, and sometimes almost square.^ Most of the bucklers were curiously adorned with all forts of figures of birds and beasts, as eagles, lions ; nor of these only, but of the gods, of the celestial bodies, and all the works of nature ; which custom was derived from the heroic times, and from them communicated to the Grecians, Romans, and Barbarians.

Votive Bucklers. Those consecrated to the gods, and hung up in their temples, either in commemoration of some hero, or as a thanksgiving for a victory obtained over an enemy; whose bucklers, taken in war, were offered as a trophy.

buckniiam.c:
BUCKNIIAM, or Buckenham, a market-town of Norfolk, about nine miles east of Thetford: E. long. i° *io', N. lat. 520 30'.

B.UCKOR, a province of the E. Indies, situated on the river Indus, having the province of Multan on the north, and Tatta on the south.

buckram.c:
BUCKRAM, in commerce, a sort of coarse cloth made of hemp, gummed, calendered, and dyed fevers] colours. It is put into those places of the lining of a garment, which one would have stiff, and to keep their forms. It is also used in the bodies of womens gowns ; and it often fer vesta make wrappers to cover cloths, ferges, and such other merchandises, in order to preserve them and keep them from the dust, and their colours from fading. Buckrams are sold wholesale by the dozen of small pieces or remnants, each about four ells long, and broad according to the pieces fu,m Which they are cut. Sometimes they use new

pieces of linen cloth to make buckrams, but mofti commonly old sheets and old pieces of fails.

Carrick buckrams pays a duty of s^'Ld. the short piece ; whereof is repaid on exporting it.

Eaftcountry buckram pays is. 2-i^yd. the roll or half-piece ; whereof is. -s%5ad. is drawn back. French, buckram pays 1 1.' 13s. ioTro*3d. the dozen pieces ; whereof il. 00s. 1 ,*oa d. is repaid. Fine German buckrams pays 2 s. 4X75^d. the piece; whereof 2 s. tic^dis drawn back on exportation.

buckstall.c: BUCKSTALL, a toil to take deer, which must not be kept by any body that has not a park Of his own, under penalties.

bucolic.c: BUCOLIC, in ancient poetry, a kind of poem relating to shepherds and country affairs, which, according to the most generally received opinion, took its rife in. Sicily. Bucolics, fays Vossius, have some conformity with comedy.' Like it, they are piiftures and imitations of ordinary life ; with this difference, however, that comedy represents the manners of the inhabitants of cities, and bucolics the occupations of country people. Sometimes, continues he, this last poem is in form of a monologue, and sometimes of a dialogue. Sometimes there is af sion in it, and sometimes only narration ; and sometimes it is composed both of action and narration. The hexameter verse is the most proper for bucolics in the Greek and Latin tongues. Moschus, Bion, Theocritus, and Virgil, are the most renowned of thfc ancient bucolic poets.

bud.c:
BUD, among gardeners, that part of a feed which first begins to sprout, or rather the leaves first put forth : These in some plants are two ; in others, four ; and in others again, six, or even more.

Bud is also used for the sprout sion whence a branch arises.

Bud, in country-affairs, likewise denotes a weaned calf of the first year ; so called, because the horns are then in the bud.

buda.c: BUDA, the capital of lower Hungary, about 130 miles south-east of Vienna: It ftarfds on the side of a hill, on the south-weft side of the Danube, and is well fortified and defended by a castle, esteemed one of the strongest fortresses in Hungary : E. long. 19* 20 , N. lat. J2° 25'.

buddesdale.c: BUDDESDALE, a market town of Suffolk, about thirteen miles north-east of Bury : E. long. i° ic/, and N. lat. 52" 25'.

buddle.c: BUDDLE, in mineralogy, a large square frame of • boards, used in waftiingthe tin ore. See Washing.

buddleia.c: BUDDLEIA, in botany, a genus of the tetrandria monogynia class. The calix and corolla are each divided into four parts ; the stamina are inserted into the receptacle ; the capsule has four cells, and contains many feeds. The species are two, viz. the occidentalism and americana, both natives of America.

buddling.c:
BUDDLING, the a<st of cleansing, or washing any ore. See Washing.

BUDGE -barrels, among engineers, small barrels well hooped, with only one head ; on the other end is nailed a piece of leather, to draw together upon firings like a purse. Their use is for carrying powder along

■^ith

B U F ( 687 ) BUI

with a gun or mortar, being lefs dangerous, andeafier carried, than whole barrels. They are likewise used upon a battery of mortars, for holding meal-powder.

budingen.c:
BUDINGEN, the capital of a county of the same name in Germany, situated in the circle of the upper Rhine, about twenty miles north-east of Frankfort.

BUDOAj a city of Dalmatia, situated on the gulf of Venice, in 190 20 E. long, and 420 ijy N. lat.

It is a bishop’s fee.

budweis.c:
BUDWEIS, a town of Bohemia, situated on the river Muldaw, about Txty-five miles fbuth of Prague: E. long. 140 20' , N. lat. 490.

BUDZIAC Tartary, a country subjest to the Turks,' situated on the rivers Neifteri Bog, and Nieper ; having Poland and Russia, on the north ; Little Tartary, on the east ; the Black-sea, on the south and Beflarabia, on the weft.

BUEN-AYRE. See Bonaire.

BUENOS-AYRES, one of the molt cbnfiderable Spani(h ports on the east coast of South America, situated on the southern shore, of the river Plata, and about fifty leagues from its mouth ; and yet here the river is full seven leagues broad : W. long. 6o°, S. lat 36°.

• It is a strong fortified town

BUEN-RETIRO, a palace near Madrid, belonging to the king of Spain.

buff.c:
BUFF, in commerce, a sort of leather prepared from

; the Ikiri of the buffalo, which, drefftd with oil, after the manner of shammy, makes what we call buff-skin. This makes a very confiderable article in the French, English, and Dutch commerce at Constantinople, Smyrna, and all along the coast of Africa. The Ikins of elks, oxen, and other-like animals, when prepared after the same manner as that of the buffalo, are likewise called buffs.

Of buff-skin, or buff-leather, are made a sort of coats for the horse or gens d’arms of France, bahdaliers, hests, pouches and gloves.

In France, there are feveral manufactories designed for the dressing of those sort of hides, particularly at Corbeil, near Paris ; at Niort, at Lyons, at Rone, at Etanepus, at Cone.

BUFFALO, in zoology. See Bos.

buffet.c:
BUFFET was anciently a little apartment, separated from the reft of the room by slender wooden columns, for the disposing of china, glass-ware, etc.

It is now properly a large table in a dinning room, called also a side-board, for the. plate, glasses, bottles, basons, &c. to be placed on, as well for the service of the table, as for magnificence. In houfijs of pylons of distinction in France, the buffet is a detached room, decorated with pi&ures relative to the subjest, with fountains, cisterns and vases. It is comm easy faced with marble or bronze.

buffoon.c: BUFFOON, a droll or mimic who diverts the public by hi*s pleasantries and follies.

bufo.c: BUFO, in zoology, the trivial name ofafpecies of rana. See Rana.

bufonia.c:
BUFONIA, in botany, a genus of the diandria monogynia class. The calix is four-leaved.} the petals are

1 four; and the capsule is unilocular, and contains two feeds. There is but one species, viz, the tenuifolia or bastard chick-weed, a native of Britain.

bug.c:
BUG, a river, which, taking its rife in red Russia int Poland* runs northward to Breste ; and then, turning westward, falls into the Weifel, or Viftula, below Warsaw.

Bug, or Bugg, in zoology, the English name of a species of cimex. See cimex.

bugen.c: BUGEN, a town of Japan, the capital of the kingdom of that name, in the if leaf Ximo.

bugey.c: BUGEY, a territory in France, being the south division of Breste; in Burgundy, on the frontiers of Savoy.

buggasins.c: BUGGASINS, in commerce, a name given to buckrams made of calico : these pay a duty, on importation, of is. 2-r^gd, the half' piece; whereof is. -,%^d. is drawn back on exportation.

buggers.c: BUGGERS, in ch tuch-history, the same with bulgarians. a feds of heretics which, amongst other errors, held, that men ought to believe no scripture but the New Testament ; that baptism was not necessary to infants; that husbands who conversed with their wives could, not be saved; and that an oath Was absolutely unlawful.

buggerer.c: BUGGERER, a person who is guilty of the crime of buggery. See the’ next article.

buggery.c: BUGGERY, is defined by Sir Edward Coke to be a carnal copulation against nature, either by the confusion of species, that is to say, a man or woman with a brute beast ; or fexes, as a man with a man, or man unnaturally with a woman. It is said this fin against God and nature was first brought into England by the Lombards; and anciently, according to some writers, it was punishable with hurtling ; but others say, with . burying alive. It is, by statute, felony without benefit of clergy, and is always excepted out of a general pardon.

bugia.c: BUGIA, a port-town of the kingdom of Algiers, in Africa, situated about sixty miles east of the city of Algiers ; E. long. 40, N. lat. 35 0 30'.

bugie.c:
BUGIE, a port-town of Egypt, situated on the western (hore of the Red-sea, almost opposite to Ziden, the port-town to Mecca, and about 100 miles weft of it; E. long. 36d, Ni lat. 2 2°.

BUGLE, in botany. See Adjuga,

BUGLOSS, in botany. SeeANCHUSA.

Viper's Bucloss, in botany. See Echii/m.

BUGULA, Bugle, in botany. See Adjuga.

buhl.c: BUHL, a little fortress in Swabia, about six miles southeast of Stolhoffen, and nineteen north-east of Strafburg.

building.c:
BUILDING, a fabric erected by art, either for devovotion, for magnificence, or for conveniency.

Regular Building, is that whose plan is square, the opposite (ides equal, and’ the parts disposed with symmetry.

Irregular Building, that whose plan is not contained with equal or parallel lines, either by the accident of situation, or the design of the builder, and whose parts, are not relative to one another in the elevation..

Inful ai-eel.

B U L f <588 'l B U

Infulatei Building, that which is not contiguous to any other, but is enconipalTed with streets, open squares, or the like.

Engaged Building, one surrounded with other buildings, having no front to any street or public place, nor any communication without, but by a common passage.

Interred or funk Building, one whose area is below the surface of the place on which it stands, and of which the lowed courses of done are concealed.

Building is aiso used for the art of cond ru&ing and railing an edifice ; in which sense it comprehends as well the expences, as the invention and execution of the design.

As for the materials of buildings, they are either done, as marble, free-done, brick for the walls, mortar, <bc. or of wood, as fir, cypress, cedars for pillars of upright ufes, oak for summers, beams, and crop-work, or for joining and conne&ion. See Architecture. ,

bul.c: BUL, in die ancient Hebrew chronology, the eighth month of the ecclefiadical, and the second of the civil year ; it has since been called Marshevan, ind answers to our October.

bulac.c:
BULAC, a town of Egypt, situated on the ead ern Ihore of the river Nile, about tWo miles wed of Grand Cairo, of which it is the porttown, and contains about four thousand families; E. long. 320, and N. lat. 30°.

It is a place of great trade, as all the vedets going up and down the Nile make some day here : it is aiso in this place that they cut the banks of die Nile every year, in order to fill their canals, and overflow the neighbouring grounds, without which the foil would produce neither grain nor herbage.

bulafo.c: BULAFO, a musical indrument confiding of feveral pipes of wood, tied together with thongs of leather so as to form a small interdice between each pipe. It is used by the negroes of Guinea.

bulb.c:
BULB, or Bulbous root, in th« anatomy of plants, expresses a root of a round or roundish figure, and usually furniflied with fibres at its base.

Bulbous roots are said to be solid, when composed of one uniform lump of matter; tunicated, when formed of multitudes of coats, surrounding one another; fquamofe, when composed of, or covered with lesser flakes ; duplicate, when there are only two to each plant ; and aggregate, when there is a congeries of such roots to each plant.

BULBOCASTANUM, in botany. SeeBuNiuM.

bulbocodium.c:
BULBOCODIUM, in botany, a genus of the hexandria monogynia class. The corolla is shaped like a tunnel, and consids of five petals; the claws of the petals are narrow. There is but one species, viz. the vernum, a native of Spain.

BULBOSE. See Bulb.

BULEUTfE, in Grecian antiquity, were magidrates answering to the decuriones among the Romans. See Decurio.

bulgar.c:
BULGAR, the capital of the province of Bulgar, in

Russia, situated on the river Wolga; E. long. ji°, and N. lat 540.

bulgaria.c:
BULGARIA, a province of Turky in Europe, bounded by the river Danube, which divides it from Wallachia and Moldavia on the north, by the Black Sea on the ead, by Romania on the south, and by Servia on the wed. Its chief city is Nicopolis.

Bulgarian language , the same with the Sclavonic.

bulimy.c:
BULIMY, a disease in which the patient is asse&ed with an insatiable and perpetual defire of eating ; and, unless he is indulged, he often falls into fainting fits. It is also called fames canina, canine appetite.

BUL1THUS, a done found either in the gall-bladder, or in the kidneys and bladder of an ox. See Bos.

BULK of a flip, the whole content in the hold for the dowage of goods.

Bulk-heads are partitions made athwart the ship with boards, by which one part is divided from the other ; as the great cabin, gun-room, bread-room, and feveral other divisions. The bulk-head afore is the partition between the fore-candle and gratings in the head.

BULL, in zoology. See Bos.

Bull, in adorn omy. See Astronomy, p. 486,

487.

Bull’s-eye, among seamen, a small, obscure, sublime . cloud, ruddy in the middle, that sometimes appears to mariners, and is the immediate forerunner of a great storm at sea.

Bull-finch, in ornithology. SeeLoxiA.

Bull-frog, in zoology, See Rana.

Bull-head, in ichthyology. SeeCoTTUs.

Bull, among ecclesiastics, a written letter, dispatched, by order of the pope, from the Roman chancery, and fealed with lead, being written on parchment, by which it is partly didinguilhed from a brief. See the article Brief.

It is a kind of apodolical rescript, or edi<3, and is chiefly in use in matters of judice or grace. If the former be the intention of the bull, the lead is hung by a hempen cord ; if the latter, by a silken thread. It is this pendent lead, or feal, which is, properly speaking, the bull, and which is impressed, on one side, with the heads of St. Peter and St. Paul, and on the other with the name of the pope and the year of his pontificate. The dmll is written in an old, round, gothic letter, and is divided into five parts, the narrative of the fa<d, the Conception, the clause, the date, and the salutation, in which the pope dyses himself servus fervor um, i. e. the servant ©f servants.

These indruments, besides the lead hanging to them, have a cross, with some text of scripture, or religious motto, about it. Bulls are granted for the consecration of bishops, the promotion to benefices, and the celebration of jubilees, &c.

Bull in coena Domini, a particular bull read every year, on the day of the Lord’s supper, or Maundy Tburfday, in the pope’s presence, containing excommunications and anathemas against heretics, and all who di curb or nppofe the jurisdiction of the holy fee.

After

B U L (

After the reading of the bull, the pope throws a burning torch into the public place, to denote the thunder of this anathema.

Golden Bull, an edict, or imperial constitution, made by the emperor Charles IV . reputed to be the magna charta, or the f undam ental law of the German empire.

It is called golden, because it has a golden fed, in the form of a pope’s bull, tied with yellow and red cords of silk : upon one side is the emperor represented fitting on his throne, and on tit other the Capitol of Rome, It is also called Caroline, on Charles IV’s account. Till the publication of the golden bull, the form and ceremony of the election of an emperor were dubious and undetermined, and the number of the electors not fixed. This solemn edi<st regulated the functions, rights,, privileges, and pre-eminences of the electors. The original, which is in Latin, on vellum, is preserved at Frankfort: this ordonnance, containing thirty articles, or chapters, was approved of by all the princes of the empire, and remain still in force.

bulla.c:
BULLA, in zoology, a genus belonging to the order of vermes testaceae. It is an animal of the snail-kind : The st sell consists of one valve, convoluted, and without any prickles ; the aperture is narrow ish, oblong, longitudinal, and entire at the base; the columella is smooth and oblique. There are twenty-three species, moll of them natives of the Asiatic and Atlantic oceans.

BULL M, in Roman antiquity, ornaments at first given only to the sons of noblemen ; though afterwards they became of more common use. This ornament was first given by Tarquinius with the prsetexsa to his fon, who had, with his own hand, at fourteen years of age, killed an enemy. Thus we find the bulla was a sign of triumph. Macrobius relates, that the children of freed men were allowed to wear the prxtexta, and, instead of the golden bulla, a leathern one, about their necks : Those bullae were made hollow within to inclose amulets against envy, &c. When the youth arrived at fifteen years of age, they hung up their bullae about the necks of their gods lares. We are farther informed, that the bullae were not only hung about the necks of young men, but of horses also.

I3ULLEN, a term used by country people for hempftalks peeled.

bullet.c: BULLET, an iron or leaden ball, pr Ihot, wherewith fire-arms are loaded. See Ball.

bullion.c:
BULLION, uncoined gold or silver in the mafs.

Those metals are called so, either when smelted from the native ore, and not perfectly refined; or when they are perfectly refined, but melted down in bars or ingots, or in any unwrought body, of any degree of fineness.

When gold and silver are in their purity, they are so soft and flexible, that they cannot well be brought into any fashion for use, without being first reduced and hardened with an alloy of some other baser metal.

To prevent these abides, which some might be Vol. I. Numb. 29. 3

689 ) BUN

tempted to commit in the making of such alloys, the legislators of civilized countries have ordained, that there shall be no more than a certain proposition of a baser metal to a particular quantity of pure gold cr silver, in order to make them of the fineness of what is called the standard gold or silver of such a country.

According to the laws of England, all forts, of wrought plate in general, ought to be made to the legal standard; and the price of our standard gold and silver is the common rule whereby to set a value on their bullion, whether the same be in ingots, bars, dull, or in foreign specie : whence it is ea(y to conceive that the value of bullion cannot be ex dally known, without being first allayed, that the exact quantity of pure metal therein contained may be determined, and consequently whether ic be above or below the standard.

Silver and gold, whether coined or uncoined, (tho* used for a common njeafure of other things), are no lefs a commodity, than wine, tobacco, or cloth ; and may, in many cafes, be exported as much to the national advantage as any other commodity.

bullock.c:
BULLOCK, the same with an ox, or gelded bull. See Bos.

BULLY-tree, in botany. See ChrysophyllUm.

bultel.c: BULTEL, a term used to denote the refuse of meal after dressing, or the cloth wherein it is dressed, otherwise called buster-cloth.

bulwark.c: BULWARK, in the ancient fortification. See Rampart.

bumicilli.c: BUMICILLI, a religious sect of Mahometans in Egypt and Barbary, who pfetend to fight with devils, and commonly appear in a fright and covered with wounds and bruises. About the full moon they counterfeit a combat in the presence of all the people, which lafts for two or three hours, and is performed with aflagaias, or javelins, till they fall down quite spent ; in a little time, however, they recover their spirits, get up, and walk away.

bungay.c:
BUNGAY, a market-town of Suffolk, situated on the river Wavenny, about thirty-two miles north-east of Bury: E. Ion. i° 35', and N. lat. 5 2° 35'.

BUNGO, or Bongo. See Bongo.

bunias.c: BUNI AS, in botany, a genus of the tetradynamia fill* quota class. The pod is deciduous, quadrangular, and the angles are Unequal and terminate in (harp points. There are four species, only one of which, viz. the dak ile, oY sea-rocket, is a native of Britain.

bundle.c:
BUNDLE, a collection of things wrapped up together. Of baste-ropes, harness-plates, and glover’s knives, ten make a bundle ; of hamburg yarn, twenty flceans ; of basket-rods, three feet about the band.

B.UNIUM, in botany, a genus of the pentandria dingy-r nia class. The corolla is uniform ; the umbella is thick; and the fruit is oval. There is but one species, viz. the bulbocastanum, earth-nut, kipper-nut, pig-nut, or hawk-nut, a native of Britain.

bunk.c:
BUNK, or Bunken, in the materia medica. See LeuCACANTHA.

BUNT of a fail , the middle part of it, formed designedly into a bag or cavity, that the fail may gather 8 M more

B U P' ( 600 ) BUR

more wind. It is used mostly in top-fails, because courses are generally cut square, or with but small allowance for bunt or compass. The bunt holds much leeward wind, that is, it hangs much to, leeward.

Bunt lines are small lines made fall to the bottom of the fails, in the middle part of the bolt-rope, to a cringle, and so are reeved through a small block, feized to the yard. Their use is to trice up the bunt of the fail, for the better furling it up.

bunting.c: BUNTING, in ornithology, the English name of a species of fringilla. See Fringilla.

buntingford.c: BUNTINGFORD, a market town of Hertfordlhire, about twelve miles north of Hertford : W. long. 5', and N. lat. 510 55'.

buntzlau.c: BUNTZLAU, or Buntzel, the name of two towns in Germany: the old town is situated on the river Elbe, and new town, which is become the mod confiderable, upon the Gizare, eight leagues from Lignitz, in i6° 26' E. long, and ji° 12' N. latitude. There is likewise a town of that name in Silesia.

buono.c: BUONO, as tempo-buono, in music, signifies a certain time or part of the measure, more proper for certain things than any other, as to end a cadence or pause, to place a long syllable or syncoped dissonance, concord, isc. In common time of four times to a bar, the first and third is one buono tempo, as the second and last are called tempo di cattiva.

buoy.c:
BUOY, at sea, a short piece of wood, or a close-hooped barrel, fattened so as to float dire&ly over the anchor, that the men, who go in the boat to weigh the anchor, may know where it lies.

Buoy is also a piece of wood, or cork, sometimes an empty calk, well closed, swimming on the surface of the water, and fattened, by a chain or cord, to a large stone, piece of broken cannon, or the like, serving to mark the dangerous places near a coast, as rocks, shoals, wrecks of vessels, anchors, ire. ■

There are sometimes, instead of -buoys, pieces of wood placed in form of masts, in conspicuous places; and sometimes large trees are planted in a particular manner, in number two at lead, to be taken in a right line, the one hiding the other, so as the two -may appear to the eye no more than one.

Stream the Buoy is to let the anchor fall while the Ihip has way.

To buo y up the cable is to fatten some pieces of wood, barrels, ire. to the cable, near the anchor, that the cable may not touch the ground, in cafe it be soul or rocky, led it IhouldT be fretted and cut off.

buphaga.c:
BUPHAGA, in ornithology, a genus belonging to the order of pices. The beak is streight and quadrangular ; the mandibles are gibbous, entire, and the gibbosity is greater on the outside. The feet are of the ambulatory kind. The body is grayish above, and of a dirty yellow below ; the tail is shaped like a wedge. It is a native of Senegal ; and frequently perches upon oxen, and picks but the worms from their backs.

1UPHTHAJLMUM, a genus of the syngenesia polygamia superflua class. The receptacle is paleaceous ; the margin of the pappus is obsolete; the fides of the feeds are marginated ; and the stigmata of the hermaphrodite floscules are undivided. The species are ten, none of which are natives of Britain.

bupleurum.c: BUPLEURUM, in botany, a genus of the pentandri.i digynia class. The involucrum of the umbelss is large and five-leaved; the fruit is striated, compressed, and roundish. The species are seventeen, only two of which are natives of Britain, viz. the rotund folium, or thorow-wax; and the tenuilfimum, or the lead hare’s-ear.

buprestis.c: BUPRESTIS, in zoology, a genus of infe&s belonging to the order of coleoptera. The feelers are like bottles, and about the length of the bread ; the lead is half retraced into the thorax. There are twenty-seven species of this inst del, most of them natives of the Indies.

buquoi.c: BUQUOI, a town of Artois, in the French Netherlands, situated on the confines of Picardy: E. long. 2° 40', and N. lat. 50° 12'.

bur.c: BUR, a broad ring of iron, behind the place made for the hand on the spears used formerly in tilting, which bur was brought to red, when the tilter charged his spear.

burbas.c: BURBAS, in commerce, a small coin at Algiers, with the arms of the dey struck on both fides : it is worth half an asper. %

burchausen.c: BURCHAUSEN, a town of Germany, in the lower Bavaria, situated on the river Salt2 : E. long. 130 2 and N. lat. 4S0 5'.

burden.c:
BURDEN, or burdon, in music, the drone or bals, and the pipe or firing which plays it : Hence that part

- of a song, that is repeated at the end of every stanza, is called the burden of it.

A chord which is to be divided, to perform the intervals of music, when open and undivided, is also called the burden.

Burden of a ship is its contents, or number of tons it will carry. The burden of a Ihip may be determined thus : multiply the length of the keel, taken within board, by the breadth of the Ihip, within board, taken from the midship-beam, from plank to plank, and multiply the prod nest by the depth of the hold, taken from the plank below the keelson, to the under part of the upper deck plank, and divide the last produdl by 94, then the quotient is the content of the tonnage required. See Freight.

burdo.c: BURDO, that kind of mule produced between a horse and a Ihe-ass. See Mule.

burdock.c: BURDOCK, in botany, the English name of the xanthium. See Xanthium.

burdugno.c: BURDUGNO, a town of the Morea, situated on the river Vafilipotomo, near Mifitra.

burial.c:
BURIAL, the interment of a deceased person.

The rites of burial are looked upon in all countries, and at all times, as a debt so sacred, that such as negle&ed to jdifcharge it were thought accursed : Hence the Romans called them jujla , and the Greeks \notni* via*, dikvia , hofia,~\ &c. words implying the inviolable obligations which nature has laid upon the living to take care of the obsequies of the dead. Nor are we to wonder, that the ancient Greeks and Romans were extremely solicitous about the interment of their deceased friends, since they were strongly persuaded, that their souls could not be admitted into the Elysian fields till their bodies were committed to the earth ; and if it happened that they never obtained the rites of burial, they were excluded from the happy mansions -for the term of an hundred years. For this reason it was confidered as a duty incumbent upon all travellers who should meet with a dead body in their way, to call dust or mould upon it three times, and of these three handfuls, one at least was cast upon the head. The ancients likewise confidered it as a great misfortune if they were not laid in the sepulchres of their fathers ; for which reason, such as died in foreign countries had usually their ashes brought home, and interred with those of their ancestors. But notwithftandiDg their great care in the burial of the dead, there were some persons whom they thought unworthy of that last office, and to whom therefore they refused it : Such . were, 1. Public or private enemies. 2. Such as betrayed, or confpiied against their country. 3. Tyrants, who were always looked upon as enemies to their country. 4. Villains guilty of sacrilege. 5. Such as died in debt, whose bodies belonged to their creditors. And, 6. Some particular offenders, who suffered capital punishment.

Of those who were allowed the rites of burial, some were distinguished by particular circumstances of disgrace attending their interment: Thus persons killed by lightening were buried apart by themselves, being thought odious to the gods; those who wafted their patrimony, forfeited the right of being buried in the sepulchres of their fathers; ard those who were guilty

BUR ( <5o2 ) BUR

of self-murder were privately deposited in the ground, without the accustomed solemnities. Among the Jews, the privilege of burial was denied only to self-murderers, who were thrown out to rot upon the ground. In the Cliriftian church, though good men always desired the privilege of interment, y t they were not, like the heathens, so concerned for their bodies, as to think it any detriment to them, if either the barbarity of an eoemy, or some other accident, deprived them of this privilege. The primitive Christian church denied the more foienin rites of burial only to unbaptized persons, felfmurclerers, and excommunicated persons who continued obilinate and impenitent, in a manifest contempt of the church’s censures.

The place of burial among the Jews was never particularly determined. We find they had graves in the town and country, upon the highways, in gardens, and upon mountains. Among the Greeks, the temples were made repositories for the dead in the primitive ages ; yet the general custom in latter ages, with them, as well as with the Romans and other heathen nations, was to bury their dead without their cities, and chiefly by the highways. Among the primitive Chrillians, burying in cities was not allowed for the first three hundred years, nor in churches for many ages after, the dead bodies being first deposited in the atrium or church yard, and porches and porticos of the church : hereditary burying-places were forbidden till the 12th century. As to the time of burial, with all the ceremonies accompanying it, fee the article Funeralrites.

burlesque.c:
BURLESQUE, a species of composition, which, tho’ a great engine of ridicule, is not confined to that subject ; for it is clearly distinguishable into burlesque that excites laughter merely, and burlesque that excites derision or ridicule. A grave subject, in which there is no impropriety, may be brought down by a certain colouring so as to be risible, as in Virgil Traveftie ; the author first laughs at every turn, in order to 'make his readers laugh. The Lutrin is a burlesque poem of the other fort, laying hold of a low and trifling incident to expose the luxury, indolence, and contentious spirit of a set r.f monks. Boileau, the author, turns the subject into ridicule by dressing it in the heroic style; and affecting to confider it as of the utmost dignity and importance. Though ridicule is the poet’s aim, he always carries a grave face, and never once bewrays a smile. The opposition between the subject and the manner of handling it, is what produces the ridicule ; and therefore, in a composition of this kind, -no image professedly ludicrous ought to have quarter, because such images destroy the contra il.

Though the burlesque that aims at ridicule, produces its effects by elevating the style far above the subject, yet the poet ought to confine himself to such images as are lively, and readily apprehended. A strained elevation, soaring above the ordinary reach of fancy, makes not a pleasant impression. The mind is soon disgusted by being kept long on the stretch. Machinery may be employed in a burlesque poem, such as the Lutrin, the Dispensary, or HuJibras, with more success and propriety than in any other species of poetry. For burlesque poems, though they assume the air of history, give entertainment chiefly by their pleasant and ludicrous pictures: It is not the aim of such a poem to raise sympathy; and for that reason, a strict imitation of nature is not necessary. And hence, the more extravagant the machinery in a ludicrous poem, the more entertainment it affords.

Burning, in antiquity, a way of disposing of the dead, much pradlifed by the ancient Greeks and Romans, and still retained by feveral nations in both the East and Weft Indies.

Euftathius assigns two reasons why burning came to be of so general use in Greece ; the first is, because bodies were thought to be unclean after the soul’s departure.

parture, and therefore were purified with fire. The second reason is, that the soul, being separated from the gross and una stive matter, might be at liberty to take its slight into heaven. The body was, rarely burnt without company, for besides the various anir-als they threw upon the pile, we seldom find a man of quality cojifumed without a number of Haves and captives, which, in barbarous times, they used to murder for that purpose : and in some parts of the East Indies it is customary, at this day, for wives to throw themselves into the funeral pile with their deceased husbands. At the funerals of emperors, generals, <bc. who had their arms burnt with them, the soldiers made procession three times round the funeral pile with shouts and trumpets, to express their respect to the dead. During the burning alio, the dead person’s friends flood by, called on the deceased, and poured out libations of wine, with which, when the pile was burnt down, they extinguished the remains of the fire ; and having collected the bones of the deceased, washed them with • wine, and anointed them with oil. When the bones were discovered, they gathered the allies that lay close to them, and both were reposited in urns, either of wood, stone, earth, silver, or gold, according to the quality of the deceased. Burning of colours, among painters. There are feveral colours that require burning; as first, lampblack, which is a colour of so greasy a nature, that, except it is burnt, it will require a long time to dry.

The method of burning, or rather drying, lampblack, is as follows : Put it into a crucible over a clear fire, letting it Femain till it be red hot, or so near it that there is no' manner of smoke arises from it.

Secondly, Umber, which if it be intended for colour fgr a horse, or to be a shadow for gold, then burning fits it for both these purposes.

In order to burn umber, you must put it into the naked fire, in large lumps, and not take it ojat till it is thoroughly red hot ; if you have a mind to be more curious, put it into a crucible, and keep it over the fire till it be red hot.

Ivory also must be burnt to make black, thus : fill two crucibles with shavings of ivory, then clap their two mouths together, and bind them fast with an iron wire, and lute the joints close with clay, fait, and horse-dung, well beaten together ; then set it over the fire, covering it all over with coals: let it remain in the fire, till you are sure that the matter inclosed is thoroughly red hot : then take it out of the fire.; but do not open the crucibles till they are perfectly

Burning bush, that bush wherein the Lord appeared to Mofes at the foot of mount Horeb, as he was feeding his father-in-law’s flocks.

As to the person that appeared in the bush, the text fays, “ That the angel of the Lord appeared unto him in a flame of fire, out of the middle of the bush but whether it was a created angel, speaking in the person of God, or God himself, or (as the mod received opinion is) Chridthe Son of God, has been matter of some controversy among the learned. Thole who suppose it no. more than an angel, seem to imply that it would be a diminution of the maja dy of God, to appear upon every occasion, especially when he has such a number of celedial ministers, who may do the business as well. But cOrifidering that God is present every where, the notification of his presence by some outward sign in one determinate place, (which is all we mean by his appearance), is in our conception lefs laborious (if any thing laborious could be conceived of God) than a delegation of angels upon every turn from heaven, and seems in the main to illudrate rather than debase the glory of his nature and exist ence. But however this be, it is plain that the angel here spoken of was no created being, from the whole context, and especially from his faying, “ I am the Lord God, the. Jehovah,.” <bc. since this is not the language of angels, who are always known to expfefs themselves in such humble terms as these, “ I am sent from . God ; I am thy fellow-servant,” <bc. It is a vain pretence to say, that an angel, as God’s ambassador, may speak in God’s name and person ; for what ambassador of any. prince evSr yet said, “ I am the king,?” Since therefore no aDgel, without the. guilt

of blasphemy, could assume these titles'; and since neither God the Father, nor the Holy Ghod, are ever called by the name of abgel, i. e. ameflenger, or person sent, whereas God the Son is galled by the prophet Malachi, (chap. iii. 1.), “ The angel of the covenant it hence seems to follow, that this angel of the Lord was God the Son, who might very properly be called an angel, because in the fulness of time he was sent into the world in our flesh, as a me danger from God, and might therefore make these his temporary apparitions, presages and forerunners, as it were, of his more sole inn million.

The Mahometans believe, that.one of Mofes’s (hoes, put off by him as he drew near the burning hush, was placed in the ark of the covenant, in order to preserve the memory of this miracle.

bushel.c:
BUSHEL, a measure of capacity for dry things, as grain, fruits, dry pulse, <bc containing four pecks, or eight gallons, or one-eighth of a quarter.

A bushel, by 12 Henry VII. c. 3. is to contain eight gallons of wheat ; the gallon eight pounds of tr oyweigh t ; the ounce twenty derlings, and the sterling thirty two grains, or corns of wheat growing in the midd of the ear.

At Paris, the bushel is divided into two half bushels ; the half bushel into two quarts ; the quart into two half quarts ; the half quart into two li trans ; and the liter on into two half li trans. By a sentence of the proved of the merchants of Paris, the bushel is to be eight inches two lines and a half high, and ten inches in diameter ; the quart four inches nine lines high, and six inches nine lines wide ; the half quart four inches three lines high, and five inches diameter ; the liter on three inches and a half high, and three inches ten lines in diameter. Three bushels make a minot ; six, a mine ; twelve, a septi er ; and an hundred and forty-four, a mud. In other parts of France the bushel varies.

Oats are measured in a double proportion to other grains, so that twenty-four bushels of oats make a septi er, and 288 a mud. The bushel of oats is divided into four picot ins, the pico tin into two half quarts, or four li trans. For fait, four bushels make one minot, and six a septi er ; for coals, eight bushels make one minot, sixteen a mine, and 320 a mud ; for lime,, three bushels make a mot, and forty-eight, minots a mud.

buskin.c:

It was of a quadrangular form, and the foie was so thick, as that, by means thereof, men of the ordinary stature might be raised to the pitch and elevation of the heroes they personated. buss.c:
BUSS, in maritime affairs, a small sea-vessel, used by us and the Dutch in the herring-fi fiery, commonly from forty-eight to sixty tons burden, and sometimes more : A bufs has two small (beds or cabins, one at the prow, and the other at the stern ; that at the prow ferves for a kitchen.

Every bufs has a matter, an assistant, a mate, and Teamen in proportion to the vessel’s bigness : the matter commands in chief, and without his express order the nets cannot be cast, nor taken up ; the assistant has the command ascer him ; and the mate next, whose business is to see the seamen manage their rigging in a proper manner, to mind those who draw in their nets, and those who kill, gut, and cure the herrings, as they are taken out of the sea : The seamen do generally engage for a whole voyage in the lump. BUSTUARlfE moech^e, according to feme, women that were hired to accompany the funeral, and lament the loss of the deceased : but others are of opinion, that they were rather the more common prostitutes, that flood among the tombs, graves, and other such lonely places.

butcher.c:
BUTCHER, a person who {laughters cattle for the use of the table, or who cuts up and retails the same.

Among the ancient Romans, there were three kinds of elfabliftied butchers, whose office was to furniffi the city with the necessary cattle, and to take care of preparing and vending their fief fi. The fuar ii provided' hogs; the pecuarii or boarii, other cattle, especially oxen; and under these was a subordinate class, whose: office was to kill, called lanii, and carnifices. To exercise the office of butcher among the Jews with dexterity, was of more reputation than to understand the liberal arts and sciences. They have a book concerning shamble-constitution ; and in cafe of any difficulty, they apply to some learned rabbi for advice : nor was any allowed to practise this art, without a lic ence in form; which gave the man, upon evidence: of his abilities, a power to kill meat, and others to eat what he killed ; provided he carefully read every week for one year, and every month the next year, and once a quarter during his life, the constitution above mentioned. We have some very good laws for the better regulation and preventing the abuses corn* • mitted by butchers. A butcher that sells swine’s flesh meazled, or dead of the murrain, for the first offence fliall be amerced ; for the second, have the pillory ; for the third, be imprisoned and make fine; and for the fourth, abjure thu town. Butchers not felling .meat at reasonable prices, iii all forfeit double the value, leviable by warrant of two justices of the peace. butter.c:
BUT TER, a fat undhious substance, prepared from milk by heating or churning it.

It was late ere the Greeks appear to have had any notion of butter ; their poets make no mention of it, and yet are frequently speaking of milk and cheese.

The Romans used butter no otherwise than as a medicine, never as a food.

The ancient Christians of Egypt burnt butter in their lamps instead of oil ; and in the Roman churches, it was anciently allowed, during Christmas time, to bum butter instead of oil, on account of the great consumption of it otherways.

For the making of butter, when it has been churned, open the churn, and with both hands gather it well together, take it out of the butter-milk, and lay it into a very clean bowl, or earthen pan ; and if the butter be designed to be used sweet, fill the pan with clear water, and work the butter in it to and fro, till . it is brought to -a firm consistence of itself, without any moisture. When this has been done, it must be scotched and sliced over with the point of a knife, every way as thick as possible, in order to fetch out the smallest hair, mote, bit of rag, strainer, or any thing that may have happened to fall into it. Then spread it thin in a bowl, and work it well together, with such quantity of fait as you think fit, and make it up into dishes, pounds, half pounds, see. The newer the butter is, the more wholesome and pleasant it is ; and that which is made in May, is esteemed the best.

There are as many forts of butter, as there are different milks of animals whereof to make it : That of the cow is moll in use. It is used every where, and there is hardly any sauce^made without -it. The northern people, however, make more use of it than others.
